Question: What is the PRIMARY purpose of engine oil?
Options: Cool the engine only
Lubricate moving parts and reduce friction
Clean the fuel injectors
Regulate ignition timing
Explanation: Engine oil lubricates all moving metal parts, reducing friction and heat. It also carries away contaminants and acts as a coolant supplement.

Question: A customer's oil hasn't been changed in 12,000 miles with conventional oil. What urgency level is this?
Options: Low — they have plenty of time
Moderate — mention it as a suggestion
High — recommend immediate service
Critical — engine may be damaged
Explanation: Conventional oil typically needs changing every 3,000–5,000 miles. At 12,000 miles, the oil is severely degraded and engine wear is actively occurring. This is a high urgency situation.

Question: When brake pads reach metal-on-metal contact, what additional repair is typically required?
Options: Only new brake fluid
Rotor replacement in addition to pads
Only caliper adjustment
ABS sensor replacement
Explanation: When pads wear through, bare metal grinds against the rotor, scoring it deeply. Once scored beyond minimum thickness spec, rotors must be replaced — significantly increasing repair cost.

Question: What does the term 'interference engine' mean in relation to timing belt service?
Options: The engine is louder than normal
Valve and piston paths overlap — a broken belt causes catastrophic damage
The timing belt also drives the alternator
The engine requires premium fuel
Explanation: In an interference engine, valves and pistons occupy the same space at different times. If the timing belt breaks, they collide — bending valves and potentially destroying pistons. This is why timing belt replacement before failure is critical.

Question: Why is brake fluid considered a 'hygroscopic' fluid, and why does that matter?
Options: It glows in the dark for leak detection
It absorbs water from the atmosphere, lowering its boiling point
It becomes more viscous over time
It is only used in ABS systems
Explanation: Brake fluid absorbs moisture from air. As water content rises, the boiling point drops. Under hard braking, fluid can boil and vaporize, causing the pedal to go to the floor — a condition called vapor lock.

Question: A customer says their car 'pulls to the right' and they notice uneven tire wear. What service is most likely needed?
Options: Tire rotation only
Oil change
Wheel alignment
Spark plug replacement
Explanation: Pulling to one side combined with uneven tire wear are classic indicators of wheel misalignment. Without alignment correction, tires will continue to wear rapidly on one edge.

Question: How does a clogged cabin air filter affect the HVAC system beyond air quality?
Options: It has no mechanical effect
It strains the blower motor, potentially causing premature failure
It increases fuel consumption
It affects the transmission
Explanation: A severely clogged cabin filter restricts airflow, causing the blower motor to work harder against increased resistance. This generates excess heat in the motor and can lead to premature failure ($200–$400 repair).

Question: What is the 'bounce test' used to evaluate?
Options: Tire pressure
Shock absorber and strut condition
Battery health
Brake pad thickness
Explanation: Push down firmly on a vehicle corner and release. If it bounces more than once, the shock or strut is likely worn. Properly functioning dampers should settle in one controlled motion.

Question: A customer's battery is 4 years old in Georgia summer heat. No symptoms yet. What should you recommend?
Options: Do nothing — wait for symptoms
Test the battery and discuss proactive replacement
Replace immediately without testing
Only check the alternator
Explanation: Heat dramatically accelerates battery degradation. A 4-year-old battery in a hot climate is statistically near end of life. Testing costs nothing and gives the customer data to make an informed decision — avoiding a no-start situation.

Question: How can worn spark plugs damage the catalytic converter?
Options: They increase exhaust backpressure
Misfires send unburned fuel into the exhaust, overheating and melting the catalyst
They reduce oil pressure to the converter
They have no effect on the catalytic converter
Explanation: Misfiring cylinders push raw unburned fuel into the exhaust stream. The catalytic converter tries to combust this fuel, generating extreme heat that can melt the internal honeycomb structure — resulting in a $800–$2,500 repair.

Question: What is the best way to explain tire rotation value to a cost-conscious customer?
Options: Tell them it's required by law
Explain that $30 now can save $400–$1,200 in early tire replacement
Say it makes the car safer immediately
Avoid bringing it up if they seem reluctant
Explanation: Cost-conscious customers respond to ROI framing. Tire rotation equalizes wear and can extend tire life by 50%. A $30 service protecting a $600+ tire investment is a compelling, concrete value proposition.

Question: Coolant that appears orange or has rusty particles indicates what problem?
Options: Normal color variation — nothing to worry about
Severe internal corrosion — immediate flush required
The coolant is still good
A problem only with the overflow tank
Explanation: Orange-tinged or rusty coolant means corrosion inhibitors have been fully depleted and oxidation is occurring inside the cooling system. Continuing to run this coolant accelerates damage to the water pump, thermostat, and radiator.

Question: A customer hears a clicking sound only when turning. What is the most likely cause?
Options: Worn brake pads
Worn CV axle joint
Loose lug nuts
Bad spark plugs
Explanation: Clicking or popping during turns is the classic symptom of a worn CV (constant velocity) joint. The joint's ball bearings click as they bind and release through extreme steering angles when the grease is gone.

Question: What is the most dangerous consequence of ignoring a worn ball joint?
Options: Slightly reduced fuel economy
Wheel separation while driving, causing loss of control
Mild tire wear on one edge
The A/C will stop working
Explanation: A completely failed ball joint allows the wheel to literally separate from the vehicle while driving. This causes immediate and total loss of steering — one of the most catastrophic mechanical failures possible.

Question: Why must a wheel alignment be performed AFTER replacing tie rod ends?
Options: It's optional — only needed if the customer complains
Tie rod ends set the toe angle; replacing them changes alignment geometry
Alignment is done before the repair, not after
Only the front axle needs alignment
Explanation: Tie rod ends directly set toe angle — the most critical alignment measurement. Replacing them changes the steering geometry, and failing to realign will immediately destroy the new tires from edge wear.

Question: A serpentine belt breaks while driving. What happens immediately?
Options: Only the radio stops working
Charging, power steering, and A/C all fail simultaneously; engine may overheat
The car safely slows to a stop with no other effects
Only the alternator stops charging
Explanation: The serpentine belt drives the alternator, power steering pump, A/C compressor, and often the water pump. When it breaks, all of these stop simultaneously. The battery drains, steering gets heavy, A/C dies, and the engine can overheat — all at once.

Question: What does 'GDI' stand for and why does it create a unique maintenance challenge?
Options: General Diagnostic Interface — it's a scan tool protocol
Gasoline Direct Injection — fuel sprays directly into the cylinder, bypassing intake valves, so carbon builds up faster
Gearbox Drive Interface — it's a transmission technology
Ground Distribution Indicator — an electrical system term
Explanation: GDI (Gasoline Direct Injection) sprays fuel directly into the combustion chamber rather than the intake port. This means intake valves never get washed by fuel, so carbon deposits accumulate much faster — requiring periodic induction cleaning or walnut blasting.

Question: A customer says their car hums and the noise gets louder when they turn left. Which wheel bearing is most likely failing?
Options: Left front — the noise gets louder when weight shifts left
Right front — weight shifts off the bad bearing when turning left, reducing noise briefly... wait, it gets louder
Left rear — steering doesn't affect rear bearings
Right front — turning left loads the right front bearing more
Explanation: When turning left, vehicle weight transfers to the right side. This loads the right front wheel bearing more. A bad right front bearing hums louder under increased load, so turning left (loading it more) makes it louder. The opposite — turning right — would unload it briefly.

Question: Why is differential fluid service often overlooked on AWD vehicles?
Options: AWD vehicles don't have differentials
There's no service interval — the fluid is lifetime
Most customers and even some advisors forget AWD has front AND rear differentials plus a transfer case — three fluid points
It's included in every oil change
Explanation: AWD vehicles have up to three separate gear oil service points: front differential, rear differential, and transfer case. Many advisors only think of the rear, and customers almost never know. A comprehensive AWD fluid service is a high-value conversation.

Question: A thermostat stuck in the OPEN position causes what symptom?
Options: Engine overheats rapidly
Engine runs cold — temperature gauge stays low, heater blows lukewarm air
Engine misfires under load
The A/C compressor cycles constantly
Explanation: A stuck-open thermostat allows coolant to flow to the radiator constantly, even when cold. The engine never reaches full operating temperature — the gauge stays low, fuel economy suffers (engines run richer when cold), and the heater produces only lukewarm air.
